cards.title: Password Storage: Salt, Hash, Prefer bcrypt
cards.summary: Store customer and admin credentials as salted hashes via bcrypt rather than reversible or unsalted schemes.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store platform, custom app or admin panel stores customer and staff login credentials.
steps: Require that passwords are never stored in plaintext or with a reversible encryption method that can be decrypted back to the original password; hashing is one-way by design, whereas encryption is not.
Salt and hash each password so identical passwords do not produce identical stored values; salting also defeats precomputed lookup tables.
For the hashing function, the source recommends simply using bcrypt rather than hand-rolling your own scheme — 'just use bcrypt' is called out as the good advice.
If you build on a framework that offers a built-in password hasher, prefer that maintained implementation over custom code, and verify the current recommended parameters for your framework version.
Keep authentication (verifying who a user is) separate in your mind from hashing (protecting stored secrets) and encryption (protecting data in transit or at rest) — these solve different problems.
caveats: bcrypt is the source's recommendation; other modern password-hashing functions also exist and are commonly used. Verify current guidance for your platform rather than treating bcrypt as the only acceptable choice.
Hashing protects stored passwords, not a compromised or misconfigured login endpoint.

cards.title: Ambient Authority via Cookies: Use SameSite
cards.summary: Browsers automatically attach cookies to requests for a site, which lets other origins trigger authenticated actions; SameSite cookies are the source's fix.
cards.use_when: Hardening cookie-based sessions for your storefront, customer accounts or admin panel so other sites cannot silently trigger authenticated requests.
steps: Understand 'ambient authority': the browser automatically attaches a site's cookies to requests destined for that site, so a request from another page can arrive already authenticated as your logged-in user.
This is the mechanism behind cross-site request forgery for state-changing actions — a logged-in shopper or admin visiting another page could have requests fired at your site carrying their session.
The source's stated solution is SameSite cookies: configure your session cookies with a SameSite attribute (typically Lax or Strict) so the browser withholds them on cross-site requests.

For state-changing endpoints — add-to-cart changes, address updates, payment or refund actions, admin mutations — consider requiring an explicit per-request token in addition to the session cookie, since SameSite policy and browser behavior can vary. Verify current browser SameSite defaults for your supported browsers.
Test the flows that legitimately need cross-site cookies (for example a payment provider returning to your site) before tightening the attribute, or you may break checkout.
caveats: Cookie attributes and browser SameSite defaults have changed over time and between browsers; verify against current browser documentation rather than relying on remembered defaults.
SameSite cookies reduce one class of cross-site request risk but are not a complete defense by themselves.

cards.title: Prefer Explicit Code Over Clever Code in Store Systems
cards.summary: In security-relevant store code, choose boring, plain, repetitive and explicit implementations over magical abstractions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or writing code that touches checkout, payments, authentication, refunds or customer data on your store.
steps: Adopt the source's stated preference: take boring, plain, repetitive, explicit code over 'magical' code — even though the clever version is more fun to write.
Apply this especially to security-relevant paths: authentication, session handling, pricing and discount calculation, refund and payment logic.
When a framework or library hides behavior behind convention or reflection, spell out the security-relevant behavior explicitly where practical, so a reviewer can see what actually happens.

This is a tradeoff, not an absolute: a well-maintained framework's built-in auth is often safer than custom code. The claim is specifically that among things you write yourself, explicit beats magical.
caveats: This is the source's stated opinion, not a measured rule. It should be weighed against using maintained, well-tested library implementations for security primitives.

cards.title: Make Dangerous Code Look Dangerous
cards.summary: Risky functions should have alarming names, clear documentation and should not be mixed with benign-looking operations.
cards.use_when: Naming and organizing internal APIs in your store platform — especially functions that move money, expose customer data or change account state.
steps: Give genuinely risky operations a scary, unmistakable name rather than a friendly one (a function that irreversibly deletes customer data or force-charges a card should sound like what it does).
Document the danger properly: what the function assumes, what it can destroy, and what the caller must guarantee before calling it.

Do not combine dangerous operations with benign ones in the same function or call path — the source explicitly warns against putting the two together, because callers then invoke risk without realizing it.

Apply this when designing internal tooling and admin actions: an admin 'quick fix' endpoint that can silently issue refunds or export customer data should be clearly labeled and separately permissioned.
This supports auditability: a reader skimming the code should be able to spot the dangerous operations from the names alone.
caveats: Naming is a human safeguard, not a technical control — it does not prevent misuse by a caller that ignores the warning.

cards.title: Adopt a Paranoid, Vigilant Security Mindset
cards.summary: The source treats constant paranoia and vigilance as a genuine asset when maintaining store security.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations and habits for whoever maintains your store's security posture over time — platform owner, in-house dev or agency.
steps: Treat the source's claim that 'you can never be too paranoid in security' as a cultural stance: assume something you depend on can fail or be attacked.

Translate vigilance into concrete practice rather than anxiety: keep dependency inventories, watch security advisories for your platform and payment stack, and re-check assumptions after major upgrades.
Assume inputs from customers, webhooks, third-party integrations and other systems are untrusted until validated — this is the practical expression of paranoia in an ecommerce stack.
Keep a paranoid posture toward your own past decisions too: a control that was adequate a year ago may not be adequate after a replatform or new integration.
Balance this against change management: constant churn in checkout and payment code carries its own risk, so schedule reviews rather than making unscheduled risky edits during peak trading.
caveats: Paranoia is a mindset, not a checklist; the source offers no specific procedures or benchmarks behind this advice.
Vigilance must be bounded — unbounded rewrites of working checkout code during peak season are themselves a risk.

cards.title: Smaller Packages Have Enlarged Modern Dependency Trees
cards.summary: Modern package managers enable many small packages with conflicting versions installed locally, so dependency trees and ecosystems are far larger than in older ecosystems.
cards.use_when: Assessing supply-chain and update risk for the libraries your storefront, checkout or integrations depend on.
steps: Recognize the structural change the source describes: package managers like npm and Rust's ecosystem allow a local dependency model, so conflicting versions can coexist in a folder rather than forcing global resolution.
That freedom lets authors publish much smaller units of functionality, so a single dependency can pull in a very large tree of transitive packages.
The source frames this as a security tradeoff: more code arrives from more places, so there are more parties and more maintainers in your dependency graph.
For your store, maintain an inventory of direct and transitive dependencies in your storefront, checkout and integration code, and check where each package's code actually originates.
When a dependency or advisory affects you, evaluate the whole path — a tiny package can be the entry point to a deep tree.
The source does not claim smaller packages are good or bad, only that their proliferation is a major ecosystem shift with more parties involved.
caveats: The source is describing an ecosystem trend from its own time; package manager behavior and ecosystem norms continue to change, so verify current tooling for your stack.
Dependency count alone is not a risk score — provenance, maintainership and how deeply a package sits in your checkout matter more.

cards.title: Standardized Collaboration Platforms Accelerated Code Flow
cards.summary: GitHub-style standardization means code moves faster and between more hands than in the older, per-project mailing-list era, expanding the trust surface.
cards.use_when: Evaluating the risk of third-party code, templates, plugins or themes you pull into your store from public repositories.
steps: The source contrasts older open source — where each project ran its own process, mailing list, version control and access model — with today's standardized platforms where everything is on GitHub.

The consequence it highlights is scale and velocity: code flies around constantly, more contributors participate, and the review and governance process that used to be project-specific is now often lightweight and uniform.
Translate this to your store: before adding a theme, app, plugin or library from a public repository, check who actually maintains it, how active it is and whether contributions are reviewed.
Prefer sources with a visible maintenance process you can inspect over repositories that only look popular.
When vendoring third-party code into checkout or customer-data paths, treat the speed and openness of the ecosystem as the reason for extra scrutiny, not less.
caveats: The source is describing the general open-source ecosystem shift, not prescribing a vetting checklist; the specific vetting criteria above are the ecommerce adaptation, not a result the source demonstrated.
Platform interfaces and repository features change; verify current tooling when checking maintainership signals.
